• what it was about

and explain why you enjoyed reading it.

answer:
I'd like to talk about a novel called The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter, which I read about two years ago during my summer holidays. A friend of mine lent it to me because she said it had completely changed the way she thought about family, and she turned out to be right.

The story is set on a small island in the early twentieth century. The main character is a teenage girl whose father looks after the lighthouse. When he becomes seriously ill, she has to take over his duties in secret, because at that time it was considered unacceptable for a girl to do such work. The book follows her through one long, stormy winter, and it describes how she gradually gains the respect of the island community.

There are several reasons why I enjoyed it so much. First of all, the writing is incredibly vivid. The author describes the sea, the weather and the island so precisely that I genuinely felt as if I were there. Secondly, the main character is brave but also very human. She makes mistakes and feels frightened, which made me care about her even more.

But I think the main reason it stayed with me is its message. It shows how much courage it takes to challenge other people's expectations, and it made me think about my own grandmother, who had to fight to go to university. Since then, I've recommended the book to quite a few people, and I'm actually planning to read it again this year.

Describe a person who has had an important influence on your life.

You should say:
• who this person is
• how long you have known him or her
• what this person is like

and explain why this person has had such an influence on you.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
The person I'd like to describe is my secondary school maths teacher, Mr Ito. I was his student for three years, from the age of thirteen to sixteen, and even though I graduated quite a while ago, we still exchange messages occasionally.

Mr Ito was not the kind of teacher who tried to be popular. He was quite strict about homework and deadlines, and he expected everyone to work hard. But at the same time, he was incredibly patient. If you didn't understand something, he would explain it again and again, using different examples, until it finally made sense. He also had a dry sense of humour, which made his lessons much more enjoyable than I'd expected.

The reason he had such an influence on me is that, before I joined his class, I had convinced myself that I was simply "bad at maths". I used to panic during tests and I'd almost given up. Mr Ito noticed this and offered to help me after school once a week. Gradually, he showed me that mistakes were a normal part of learning rather than a sign of failure.

By the end of my final year, maths had become one of my best subjects, and I eventually decided to study economics at university, which involves a lot of statistics. More importantly, he taught me that ability isn't fixed, and that with enough effort you can improve at almost anything. I still try to remember that whenever I face something difficult.

You should say:
• where it is
• when you went there
• what you did there

and explain why you would like to go there again.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
I'd like to talk about a small mountain village in the north of my country, which I visited about three years ago with my university hiking club. It's quite remote – you have to take two trains and then a local bus that runs only four times a day – but that's part of its charm.

We stayed there for four days in a traditional wooden guesthouse run by an elderly couple. Every morning, they served us an enormous breakfast made almost entirely from local ingredients, including vegetables from their own garden. During the day, we hiked along trails through the forests and up to a lake surrounded by peaks. The scenery was absolutely breathtaking, especially early in the morning when the mist was rising off the water.

In the evenings, we sat around chatting with the owners, who told us stories about how the village had changed over the years. Apparently, many young people have moved away to the cities, and the population is now less than half of what it used to be.

There are a few reasons why I'd love to go back. Firstly, I only saw the village in summer, and I've heard it's even more beautiful in autumn, when the leaves turn red and gold. Secondly, I felt incredibly relaxed there, with no traffic and hardly any phone signal. But mainly, I'd like to see the elderly couple again. They made us feel so welcome, and I promised them I'd return one day.

Describe a skill that took you a long time to learn.

You should say:
• what the skill is
• when you started learning it
• how you learned it

and explain why it took you a long time to learn.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
The skill I'd like to describe is swimming, which might sound surprising, because most people learn it as young children. In my case, though, I didn't learn to swim properly until I was nineteen.

When I was little, I had a frightening experience at the seaside – I was knocked over by a wave and swallowed a lot of water – and after that I developed a real fear of being in deep water. My parents tried to send me to lessons a couple of times, but I would cry and refuse to get in the pool, so they eventually gave up.

It wasn't until my first year at university that I decided to tackle the problem. Many of my friends were planning a trip to an island, and I felt embarrassed that I wouldn't be able to join them in the sea. So I signed up for adult beginner classes at the university pool. There were only five of us in the group, and the instructor was extremely patient. For the first few weeks, we didn't even swim; we just practised breathing and floating while holding on to the side.

The main reason it took so long was psychological rather than physical. Every time I put my face in the water, I felt a wave of panic, and I had to learn to stay calm. It took about six months before I could swim a full length without stopping. Looking back, it was one of the most satisfying achievements of my life, because it meant overcoming a fear I'd had for over ten years.

answer:
I'm going to talk about my e-reader, which is a small electronic device designed specifically for reading digital books. I got it about four years ago as a birthday present from my parents, who were tired of seeing piles of books all over my bedroom!

I use it almost every day. In the mornings, I read on the train on my way to work, which takes about forty minutes, and I usually read for a while in bed before going to sleep. I also take it with me whenever I travel.

There are several reasons why I find it so useful. The most obvious one is convenience. It's very light – lighter than a single paperback – but it can store thousands of books. Before I had it, I used to carry three or four heavy books in my suitcase on holiday, and now I just take this one device.

Another advantage is that the screen is designed to look like paper, so it doesn't strain my eyes the way a phone or laptop screen does. The battery also lasts for several weeks, which means I hardly ever need to charge it. I find the built-in dictionary really helpful, too, especially when I'm reading books in English. I can just touch an unfamiliar word and see its definition immediately.

Finally, and this is quite important for me, it doesn't have social media or notifications, so I can concentrate completely on reading without being distracted. In a way, it's a piece of technology that actually helps me spend less time on screens.

answer:
I'd like to describe an overnight train journey I took about five years ago, when I travelled from the capital to a city on the southern coast with my older brother. We could have flown, which would have taken just over an hour, but we decided to take the sleeper train because neither of us had ever done it before.

We left at around nine in the evening. Our compartment was tiny, with two narrow bunk beds, a little table and a window. My brother took the top bunk, and I had the bottom one. Before going to bed, we went to the dining car, where we had a surprisingly good dinner and chatted with an elderly man who had been taking the same train once a year for over forty years. He told us all kinds of stories about how the journey had changed.

I didn't sleep very much, to be honest, because the train kept stopping and starting, but I didn't mind at all. I remember lying awake and watching the lights of small towns pass by in the darkness. Then, early in the morning, the train came out of a tunnel and suddenly the sea was right there, shining in the sunrise. It was an unforgettable sight.

I think I remember this journey so clearly because it was more than just a way of getting somewhere; it was an experience in itself. It was also one of the last trips my brother and I took together before he moved abroad, so it means a lot to me.

answer:
I'd like to talk about a time when I helped an elderly woman at a train station. It happened last winter, on a very cold evening, when I was on my way home from work.

I was waiting on the platform when I noticed an old lady who looked very confused. She was holding a piece of paper and looking up at the timetable, and she seemed quite upset. So I went over and asked if she needed any help. It turned out that she was trying to get to her daughter's house in a town I'd never heard of, and her train had been cancelled because of the snow.

At first, I wasn't sure what to do. But I checked the route on my phone and found that she could take a different train and then a bus. The problem was that she had a heavy suitcase and she was quite nervous about changing trains on her own. As I had nothing urgent to do that evening, I decided to go with her as far as the next station and help her find the right bus. I also called her daughter to explain the situation, so that she could meet her mother at the bus stop.

The whole thing took about an hour and a half, and I got home quite late. But I felt really good about it. The lady thanked me again and again, and her daughter sent me a lovely message later that night. It reminded me how small actions can make a big difference to someone.

question:
Describe a festival or celebration that is important in your country.

You should say:
• what the festival or celebration is
• when it takes place
• what people do during it

and explain why it is important to people in your country.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
I'd like to talk about the New Year celebration in my country, which is probably the most important holiday of the year. Unlike in some countries, where New Year is mainly a party night, for us it's a family occasion that lasts for several days, from the thirty-first of December until about the third of January.

The preparations actually begin a few days earlier. People clean their homes thoroughly, which symbolises getting rid of the bad luck of the previous year, and they decorate the entrance with special ornaments. Many families also prepare traditional dishes in advance, each of which has a particular meaning, such as health, long life or prosperity.

On New Year's Eve, families usually gather at home to eat a special noodle dish and watch television together. At midnight, bells ring at temples all over the country. Then, on New Year's Day, people visit shrines or temples to pray for good fortune in the coming year. It's also traditional for children to receive small envelopes of money from their relatives, which, as you can imagine, is their favourite part!

I think it's important to people for a couple of reasons. Firstly, it's one of the few times in the year when everybody has a holiday at the same time, so it's a rare chance for families to get together, especially those who live in different cities. Secondly, it gives people a sense of a fresh start. Many people make resolutions and reflect on what they want to achieve. Even though lifestyles are changing, I think these traditions help people feel connected to their culture.

• where it is

answer:
The building I'd like to describe is an old castle in a city about three hours from where I live. I visited it on a school trip when I was fifteen and then again last year with a friend, and I found the second visit far more meaningful than the first.

The castle was originally built in the early seventeenth century and stands on a hill overlooking the city. What makes it particularly striking is its main tower, which is white with dark grey roofs that curve upwards at the edges. It's surrounded by thick stone walls and a wide moat, and in spring the grounds are filled with cherry trees, which makes the whole place look like a painting.

Inside, the tower has been turned into a museum. There are displays of armour, weapons and documents, and you have to climb some extremely steep wooden staircases to reach the top floor, from which you get a panoramic view of the city. What I found fascinating was learning how the castle was constructed without any nails, using only interlocking wooden joints. I also learned that, unlike many other castles, it survived wars and natural disasters almost entirely intact.

When I visited as a teenager, I was mostly interested in taking photos with my friends. But on my second visit, I felt a real sense of awe. Standing at the top, I tried to imagine the people who had lived and worked there four hundred years ago. It made me appreciate how much skill and effort went into creating something that has lasted so long.

answer:
One of the most important decisions I've ever made was to change my university major from law to computer science. I made this decision at the end of my first year, when I was nineteen.

I'd originally chosen law mainly because my parents thought it would lead to a secure, respectable career, and to be honest, I hadn't really considered any alternatives. But during my first year, I found the lectures increasingly dull. At the same time, I'd joined a programming club just for fun, and I discovered that I could spend hours writing code without noticing the time pass.

The decision wasn't easy, and I didn't make it overnight. First, I talked to students who were already studying computer science, to find out what the course was really like. Then I made an appointment with a careers adviser, who helped me compare the job prospects in both fields. I even wrote a list of pros and cons, which sounds a bit old-fashioned, but it helped me see things more clearly. The hardest part was telling my parents. I was worried that they'd be disappointed, but when I explained my reasons calmly and showed them that I'd done my research, they were surprisingly supportive.

At the time, I felt a mixture of anxiety and relief. I was nervous about starting again and about whether I'd be able to catch up with the maths. But looking back now, I'm certain it was the right choice. I genuinely enjoy what I study, and I think I've learnt that it's important to make decisions based on your own interests, not just other people's expectations.

The advert began with an elderly man living alone in a small house in the countryside. He was shown doing ordinary things – making tea, watering his plants, looking at old photographs – and you could tell he was quite lonely. Then the scene changed to a young woman in a big city, working late in an office and looking tired. At first, you didn't know how the two people were connected.

In fact, I booked a trip to see them shortly after seeing the advert, so I suppose it was quite effective!

The family member I admire most is my aunt Keiko, my mother's younger sister. She's in her early fifties now, and she lives in a small town by the sea, where she runs a bakery.

She's one of the most energetic and positive people I know. She's always laughing and telling stories, and she has a way of making everyone around her feel relaxed. At the same time, she's very determined. Once she decides to do something, nothing seems to stop her.

What she has achieved is quite remarkable. For about twenty years, she worked as an accountant in a large company in the city. She was successful, but she often said she felt that something was missing. Then, at the age of forty-five, she decided to leave her job and open a bakery, even though she had no professional training. Lots of people, including my grandparents, thought it was too risky. But she took evening classes, practised baking every weekend for a year, and eventually used her savings to rent a small shop. The first two years were very difficult, and she nearly gave up. Now, however, her bakery is one of the most popular places in the town, and she employs four people.

I admire her for several reasons. Most importantly, she showed me that it's never too late to change direction and follow your passion. She also proved that hard work and persistence can overcome difficulties. Whenever I feel nervous about trying something new, I think of her, and it gives me courage.

question:
Describe an environmental problem that affects the area where you live.

You should say:
• what the problem is
• what causes it
• how it affects people

and explain what you think should be done about it.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
The environmental problem I'd like to talk about is air pollution in my city, particularly during the winter months. I live in a large city surrounded by mountains, and on some days the air becomes so polluted that you can't even see the hills from the city centre.

There are several causes. The main one is traffic. The number of cars has increased dramatically over the last twenty years, and many of them are older vehicles that produce a lot of exhaust fumes. In addition, there are factories on the edge of the city, and in winter many households burn coal or wood for heating. Because of the city's geography, the polluted air gets trapped in the valley, especially when there's no wind.

The effects on people are quite serious. On the worst days, the authorities advise people, especially children and elderly people, to stay indoors. Many people wear masks when they go out. Doctors have reported an increase in respiratory problems such as asthma, and I know several people who suffer from coughs throughout the winter. It also affects quality of life in less obvious ways. People exercise outside less, and the grey sky can make everyone feel quite depressed.

In my opinion, a combination of measures is needed. The government should improve public transport and introduce stricter emission standards for vehicles, perhaps even banning the oldest cars from the city centre. They should also help households switch to cleaner heating, for example by providing subsidies. These changes would be expensive, but I think the health benefits would justify the cost.

I'd like to talk about a time when I was late for a job interview. It happened about a year and a half ago, when I was applying for a part-time position at a marketing company.

The interview was at ten o'clock in the morning, in an office building in the city centre. I'd planned everything carefully. I'd checked the route the night before and decided to leave home at nine, which should have given me plenty of time. Unfortunately, things didn't go as planned. About ten minutes after I got on the train, it suddenly stopped between two stations. An announcement said there was a signal problem, and we waited there for almost thirty minutes.

I started to panic. I didn't have the interviewer's phone number, only an email address, so I sent a quick email explaining the situation. When the train finally started moving again, I ran all the way from the station to the office and arrived about twenty minutes late, completely out of breath.

Luckily, the interviewer was very understanding. She said she'd seen my email and that delays happen to everyone. She gave me a few minutes to calm down and then started the interview. In the end, I actually got the job!

I felt terrible at the time – embarrassed, stressed and sure that I'd ruined my chances. But looking back, I learned two important lessons. First, I always leave much earlier for important appointments now. And second, I always make sure I have a phone number to call if something goes wrong.

You should say:
• where it is
• how you know about it
• what you would like to do there

and explain why you would like to visit this city.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
A city I've wanted to visit for a long time is Lisbon, the capital of Portugal. It's on the west coast of the country, built on a series of hills overlooking a wide river that flows into the Atlantic Ocean.

I first became interested in it a few years ago, when I watched a travel documentary about southern Europe. The presenter spent a few days walking around the old neighbourhoods, and I was struck by how colourful and lively the city looked. Since then, I've read quite a lot about it online, and a friend of mine who studied there for a semester has shown me lots of photos and told me stories about her time there.

If I went there, the first thing I'd like to do is ride one of the old yellow trams that climb up and down the steep, narrow streets. I'd also love to explore the oldest district, which apparently survived a huge earthquake in the eighteenth century, and visit some of the viewpoints, where you can see the whole city and the river at sunset. Food is another big attraction for me. I'd definitely want to try the famous custard tarts and some of the fresh seafood.

I think the main reason I want to visit Lisbon is that it seems to combine a lot of things I love: history, beautiful architecture, the sea and good food. It also looks quite relaxed compared with some other European capitals, and I like the idea of just wandering around without a fixed plan. Hopefully, I'll be able to go there after I graduate.

question:
Describe a gift you gave to someone that made them happy.

You should say:
• who you gave it to
• what the gift was
• why you chose this gift

and explain how the person felt when they received it.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
I'd like to talk about a gift I gave to my father for his sixtieth birthday last year. Sixty is quite a special birthday in my country, so I wanted to give him something meaningful, not just a tie or a bottle of wine.

In the end, I decided to make him a photo book about his life. It took me about two months to prepare. First, I secretly collected old photographs from my grandmother and my aunts, including pictures of my father as a baby, at school and on his wedding day. Then I asked his old friends and colleagues to write short messages for him. I scanned all the photos, wrote some short captions, and designed the book using a website. Finally, I had it printed with a hard cover.

I chose this gift because my father is quite a sentimental person. He often tells stories about when he was young, but many of his old photos were kept in boxes and he rarely looked at them. I also knew he didn't really need any more things, so I thought a personal gift would mean more to him than something expensive.

When he opened it at his birthday dinner, he went very quiet. He turned the pages slowly, and I could see he was trying not to cry. Then he started laughing at some of the old photos and telling everyone the stories behind them. He said it was the best present he'd ever received. Now he keeps the book on the shelf in the living room and shows it to everyone who visits.

question:
Describe something useful you learned outside school or university.

You should say:
• what you learned
• when and where you learned it
• how you learned it

and explain why it has been useful to you.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
I'd like to talk about learning basic first aid, which I did about three years ago through a weekend course run by a local volunteer organisation. I signed up mainly because my younger cousin has a serious allergy, and I wanted to know what to do if something happened when I was looking after him.

The course took place over two days in a community hall near my home. There were about fifteen people in the group, from teenagers to retired people, and the instructors were two paramedics who volunteered in their free time.

What I liked was that it was extremely practical. On the first day, we learned how to check whether someone is breathing, how to put a person in the recovery position and how to perform CPR on special training dummies. On the second day, we practised dealing with burns, cuts, choking and allergic reactions, including how to use an emergency injection pen. The instructors created realistic scenarios, and we had to respond in pairs while they watched and gave us feedback. At the end, we took a short test and received a certificate.

It's been useful in a number of ways. Most obviously, I feel much more confident when I'm looking after my cousin. But I've also actually used what I learned. Last year, an elderly man fell over in a supermarket and hit his head, and I was able to keep him calm, check his injuries and give clear information to the ambulance staff. Without the course, I think I would have just panicked. Honestly, I think everyone should learn first aid.

question:
Describe a rule (at school, at work or in society) that you think is important.

You should say:
• what the rule is
• where it applies
• what happens if people break it

and explain why you think this rule is important.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
The rule I'd like to talk about is one that my secondary school introduced when I was about fourteen: students weren't allowed to use their mobile phones at any time during the school day, including at lunchtime. Phones had to be switched off and kept in our lockers from the moment we arrived until the end of the last lesson.

When it was first announced, almost everyone was against it. We thought it was unfair and old-fashioned, and some parents complained as well, mainly because they were worried about not being able to contact their children. The school responded by allowing parents to call the school office in an emergency.

If a student was caught using a phone, it was confiscated and kept in the head teacher's office until the end of the week. For a teenager, that was a serious punishment! Repeat offenders had to attend a meeting with their parents. In practice, though, the rule was broken surprisingly rarely once people got used to it.

Looking back, I think it was a very sensible rule, for a few reasons. The most noticeable effect was on lunchtimes. Before the rule, many students sat in silence staring at their screens; afterwards, people actually talked to each other, played games outside and made new friends. Concentration in lessons also improved, because there were no notifications to distract us. And it reduced problems like cyberbullying during school hours. I think it taught me that I don't need to be connected all the time, which is something I still try to remember today.

question:
Describe a park or natural place that you enjoy visiting.

You should say:
• where it is
• what it looks like
• what you do there

and explain why you enjoy visiting this place.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
The place I'd like to describe is a large forest park on the edge of my city, about thirty minutes away by bus. It covers several square kilometres and includes woodland, a small lake and a hill with walking trails.

What I love about it is that, even though it's so close to the city, once you're inside it feels completely wild. The paths wind through tall pine and oak trees, and in some places you can't hear any traffic at all, only birds and the wind. The lake is surrounded by reeds, and there's a wooden boardwalk where you can sometimes see herons and turtles. From the top of the hill, there's a wonderful view across the whole city, which looks surprisingly small from up there.

I usually go there two or three times a month, often on Sunday mornings. Sometimes I go with friends and we have a picnic by the lake, but more often I go alone and walk for two or three hours. In autumn, I like taking photographs of the changing leaves, and in winter, when it occasionally snows, the forest is incredibly peaceful.

I enjoy visiting it mainly because it helps me relax and recharge. My life in the city is quite busy and noisy, and spending time surrounded by nature has a really calming effect on me. I find that my mind becomes clearer, and I often come up with ideas or solutions to problems while I'm walking. It's also good exercise, of course. I honestly think that having a place like this nearby makes city life much more bearable.

question:
Describe a film that made you think deeply about something.

You should say:
• what the film was
• when you watched it
• what it was about

and explain why it made you think deeply.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
I'd like to talk about a documentary called The Last Harvest, which I watched about a year ago at a small independent cinema during a film festival. I went with a friend who studies agriculture, and to be honest, I wasn't expecting much, but it ended up being one of the most thought-provoking films I've ever seen.

The film follows three farming families in different parts of the world over the course of a single year. One family grows rice, another raises cattle and the third grows coffee. Without any narrator, it simply shows their daily lives: the physical work, the worries about the weather and prices, and the moments of celebration when the harvest is successful. Gradually, it becomes clear that all three families are facing similar challenges, especially the effects of unpredictable weather and the difficulty of earning a decent income.

What made me think so deeply was the realisation of how disconnected I am from the food I eat. I buy rice and coffee every week without ever considering the people who produce them or how vulnerable their livelihoods are. There's one scene in particular that stayed with me, where the coffee farmer explains that the price he receives for an entire sack is less than the cost of a few cups in a city café.

Since watching it, I've changed some of my habits. I now try to buy products with fair-trade certification, and I've become much more conscious of food waste. More broadly, the film made me realise how important it is to question where things come from, rather than just taking them for granted.

question:
Describe a goal that you would like to achieve in the future.

You should say:
• what the goal is
• when you set this goal
• what you need to do to achieve it

and explain why this goal is important to you.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
One goal I'd really like to achieve is to run a full marathon before I turn thirty. I set this goal about eighteen months ago, after I watched my best friend finish a marathon in our city. Seeing all the runners cross the finish line, some of them in tears, was so inspiring that I decided I wanted to experience that feeling myself.

At the moment, I'm still quite far from achieving it. I've started running regularly, three times a week, and a few months ago I completed my first half marathon, which is twenty-one kilometres. It was much harder than I expected, especially the last five kilometres, but finishing it gave me a lot of confidence.

To achieve my goal, I'll need to follow a proper training plan, gradually increasing the distance of my long runs each week. I also need to improve my diet and get more sleep, because I've noticed that when I'm tired, my training suffers. Another important thing is to avoid injuries, so I've started doing strength exercises and stretching. I'm planning to enter a marathon next autumn, which gives me about a year to prepare.

This goal is important to me for a few reasons. Physically, it's a great motivation to stay healthy, because I have a desk job and I used to do very little exercise. But I think it's even more important mentally. I've never been particularly sporty, and I tend to give up on things when they get difficult. Completing a marathon would prove to me that I can achieve something challenging through patience and hard work.

question:
Describe a time when you worked successfully as part of a team.

You should say:
• what the team had to do
• who was in the team
• what your role was

and explain why the team was successful.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
I'd like to talk about a group project I did in my second year at university. We were asked to design a marketing campaign for a real local business, a family-owned bakery that wanted to attract more young customers. At the end of the semester, we had to present our ideas to the owners and our professor.

There were five of us in the team, and we were all quite different. Two of us were business students, one was studying graphic design, one was an international student from Brazil, and I was studying economics. At first, I was a bit worried, because we didn't know each other well and our schedules were very different.

My role was to research the market and the bakery's competitors. I designed a short questionnaire, collected responses from over a hundred students and analysed the results. I found out, for example, that many students didn't even know the bakery existed, because it had no online presence. The design student then created a logo and social media posts, while the others worked on the budget and the presentation.

I think we were successful for a few reasons. Firstly, we made sure everyone's role matched their strengths, so people felt confident and responsible for their part. Secondly, we communicated well. We had a group chat and met every Thursday to update each other and solve problems together. And finally, we respected each other's ideas, even when we disagreed. In the end, the owners liked our proposal so much that they actually started using some of our ideas, and we got the highest grade in the class.

question:
Describe a piece of art, such as a painting or photograph, that you like.

You should say:
• what it is
• where you saw it
• what it shows

and explain why you like it.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
The piece of art I'd like to describe is a black-and-white photograph that I saw at a photography exhibition in a city museum about two years ago. Unfortunately, I can't remember the photographer's name, but the image itself has stayed with me ever since.

The exhibition was about city life in the mid-twentieth century, and most of the photos showed busy streets, markets and factories. This particular one was quite different. It showed an elderly man sitting alone on a bench at a railway station late at night. The platform was empty, and the only light came from a single lamp above him, which created a strong contrast between the bright area around him and the deep darkness of the rest of the image. He was holding a small bunch of flowers on his lap and looking towards the tracks, as if he were waiting for someone.

What I find so powerful about it is that it tells a story without giving you the answer. You naturally start wondering who he's waiting for. Is it a wife coming home after a long journey? A child he hasn't seen for years? Or perhaps no one at all? Each time I think about it, I imagine a different story.

I also admire it technically. The composition is very simple, but the use of light and shadow creates a feeling of both loneliness and hope. I bought a postcard of it at the museum shop, and it's now on the wall above my desk. Whenever I look at it, it reminds me that the most moving art is often the quietest.

answer:
The object I'd like to describe is an old wooden clock that belongs to my family. It originally belonged to my great-grandfather, so it's probably around a hundred years old.

It's a wall clock, about sixty centimetres tall, made of dark wood with a glass door at the front. Behind the glass, you can see a brass pendulum swinging slowly from side to side. The face is white with black numbers, although it's turned slightly yellow over the years. Every hour, it chimes the number of times that matches the hour, and it has quite a deep, gentle sound.

According to family stories, my great-grandfather bought it when he opened his first shop, a small hardware store, and it hung on the wall there for many years. When he retired, my grandfather took it home, and when my grandparents moved into a smaller flat, they gave it to my parents. Now it hangs in the hallway of our family home, and my father winds it every Sunday morning, which is a kind of ritual for him.

I think we've kept it for so long mainly because of its sentimental value. It's not worth much money, but it connects us to family members we never met. My father says that when he hears it chime, he remembers sitting in his grandfather's shop as a child. For me, it's the sound of home – I've heard it every day of my life. Even though it sometimes runs a few minutes slow, nobody would ever think of replacing it.

Describe a time when you changed your mind about something.

You should say:
• what you changed your mind about
• when this happened
• what made you change your mind

and explain how you felt about changing your mind.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
I'd like to talk about how I changed my mind about vegetarianism. For most of my life, I was quite dismissive of it. I grew up in a family where meat was part of almost every meal, and I used to think vegetarians were being unnecessarily fussy, or that it was just a fashionable trend.

The change happened gradually over about a year, starting roughly three years ago, when I moved into a shared flat with a student from India who had been vegetarian since birth. At first, I assumed her meals would be boring, but I was completely wrong. She cooked incredibly varied and flavourful dishes using lentils, beans, vegetables and spices, and she often shared them with me.

What really changed my mind, though, was a conversation we had one evening. She didn't lecture me at all; she simply explained her reasons, which were partly cultural and partly environmental. That made me curious, so I started reading about the environmental impact of meat production, particularly the amount of land, water and greenhouse gases involved. I was genuinely shocked by some of the figures.

I didn't become fully vegetarian, but I now eat meat only two or three times a week, and I've learned to cook quite a few vegetarian dishes myself. As for how I felt, at first it was slightly uncomfortable to admit that my previous opinion had been based on prejudice rather than knowledge. But overall, I felt positive about it. I think being able to change your mind when you encounter new evidence is a sign of maturity rather than weakness.

The busiest period I can remember was about two years ago, in the final month of my university course. Several things happened at the same time, and I honestly don't know how I got through it.

Firstly, I had to finish and submit my graduation thesis, which was about fifteen thousand words long. I'd planned to finish most of it earlier, but my research took longer than expected, so I still had about a third left to write. Secondly, I had three final exams in the same two weeks. On top of that, I was working part-time at a restaurant three evenings a week, and I'd also agreed to help organise my younger sister's birthday party, which I couldn't really cancel.

To manage everything, I had to be extremely organised. I made a detailed schedule for every day, divided into blocks of time for writing, revision and work. I got up at six every morning and wrote my thesis for three hours before doing anything else, because that's when I concentrate best. I also asked my manager at the restaurant if I could reduce my shifts for a few weeks, and luckily she agreed. And I asked my cousin to take care of most of the party preparations.

During that month, I felt quite stressed and exhausted most of the time. I wasn't sleeping well, and I hardly saw my friends. But there was also a sense of satisfaction each time I completed a task and crossed it off my list. When I finally submitted my thesis, I felt an incredible sense of relief, and I learned a lot about how to manage pressure.

I'd like to talk about a short video I saw on social media a few months ago. It was shared by a friend of mine who works as a primary school teacher, and it was about a community project in a small town.

The video showed a group of elderly residents and teenagers who had been paired up to teach each other new skills. The teenagers were teaching the older people how to use smartphones – things like making video calls, sending photos and using maps – while the elderly residents were teaching the teenagers traditional skills, such as knitting, cooking regional dishes and repairing clothes. The video was only about three minutes long, but it included short interviews with both groups.

I saw it late one evening when I was scrolling through my feed, and I ended up watching it three times. Then I sent it to my mother, who later shared it with her friends.

There were several reasons why I found it so interesting. Firstly, it was such a simple idea, but it solved two problems at once: many older people feel isolated because they can't use technology, and many young people have never learned practical skills from older generations. Secondly, I loved seeing how the relationships developed. At the beginning, both groups looked a bit awkward, but by the end they were laughing together and clearly enjoying each other's company. One elderly woman said that video-calling her grandchildren had changed her life. Finally, it made me wonder whether a similar project could work in my own town. Most of what I see online is quickly forgotten, but this video really stayed with me.

I was with three friends, and none of us except my friend Marco had ever eaten Ethiopian food before. Marco had lived in Ethiopia for a year with his family when he was a child, so he was really excited to show us.

Instead of individual plates, there was one very large, round, flat bread called injera on a big tray, and on top of it there were lots of small piles of different stews and vegetables. To be honest, I felt a bit nervous at the beginning, because eating with my hands in a restaurant felt unusual and I was worried about making a mess. But after a few minutes, I started to really enjoy it. Sharing food from the same tray made the meal feel very friendly and relaxed, and we talked and laughed a lot. I loved the flavours, and I've been back to that restaurant several times since then. It taught me that trying new things can be really rewarding.

People can do much more than just borrow books there. Students come to study, especially before exams, when it's often difficult to find a free seat. There are free language classes for immigrants, computer lessons for older people and a weekly job club, where people can get help writing CVs and applying for jobs. Local groups, like book clubs and chess clubs, also use the meeting rooms in the evenings.

I think it's extremely useful to local people. For many families who can't afford to buy lots of books or don't have a quiet place to study at home, the library is essential. It's also one of the few places in the city where you can spend time without having to pay for anything. In addition, it brings together people of all ages and backgrounds, which I think strengthens the community. Personally, I go there at least once a week, and I'd be really sad if it ever closed.

question:
Describe a time when you lost something important.

You should say:
• what you lost
• when and where you lost it
• what you did to find it

and explain how you felt when you lost it.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
I'd like to talk about the time I lost my wallet while I was on holiday abroad. It happened about three years ago, on the second day of a trip to a big city with my friend.

We had spent the morning visiting a museum, and then we took a crowded bus to a famous market. When we arrived and I wanted to buy a drink, I realised that my wallet wasn't in my bag. I checked every pocket again and again, but it was gone. It had my cash, my bank card, my driving licence and a photo of my family in it.

At first, we went back to the bus stop and asked the people there if anyone had seen it, but nobody had. Then my friend helped me search online for the bus company's lost property office. While she was doing that, I called my bank to cancel my card, which was the most urgent thing. After that, we went to the nearest police station to report it, because I needed a police report for my travel insurance. The police officer was very kind, but he said it was unlikely I would get it back.

I felt terrible – stressed, angry with myself and a bit embarrassed. I was worried that the whole holiday was ruined. Luckily, my friend lent me some money, and the next day something amazing happened: the bus company called to say that a driver had found my wallet under a seat. Everything was still inside! I was so relieved and grateful. Since then, I've always been very careful with my things, especially on public transport.

question:
Describe an interesting conversation you had with someone you did not know.

You should say:
• who the person was
• where you had the conversation
• what you talked about

and explain why the conversation was interesting.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
I'd like to describe a conversation I had with a stranger on a long-distance bus about a year ago. I was travelling to another city for a job interview, and the journey took about five hours.

The woman sitting next to me was probably in her sixties. At first, we didn't talk at all. She was reading a book, and I was going over my notes for the interview. But after about an hour, the bus stopped at a service station, and when we got back on, she asked me if I was a student, because she'd noticed my notes. I explained that I was going to an interview for a job in environmental engineering, and that I was quite nervous.

It turned out that she was a retired engineer who had worked on water projects in several different countries. We ended up talking for almost the entire journey. She told me about building wells in villages that had never had clean water, and about the challenges of working in very different cultures. She also asked me lots of questions about my studies and gave me some advice for the interview, such as giving specific examples of what I'd done rather than just talking about my skills.

The conversation was interesting for several reasons. Firstly, her experiences were fascinating, and they showed me how much impact engineering can have on people's lives. Secondly, her advice was really useful – I used it in the interview the next day, and I actually got the job! But I think what I remember most is how unexpected it was. I'd planned to spend the journey studying quietly, but instead I had one of the most inspiring conversations of my life.

question:
Describe a time when you spent a day in the countryside.

You should say:
• where you went
• who you went with
• what you did there

and explain how you felt about spending the day in the countryside.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
I'd like to talk about a day I spent at a strawberry farm in the countryside last spring. The farm is about an hour and a half by train from my city, in an area famous for fruit growing.

I went with my older sister and her two young children, who were six and eight at the time. My sister had seen an advertisement for "pick your own" strawberries online and thought it would be a fun day out for the kids, and she asked me to come along to help.

We arrived at about ten in the morning. The farmer gave each of us a small basket and explained which rows of plants we could pick from. The strawberries were growing in long greenhouses, and the smell was amazing. The children were incredibly excited, and I think they ate more strawberries than they put in their baskets! After about an hour, we had lunch at a small café on the farm, which served homemade strawberry cakes and ice cream. In the afternoon, we walked along a path through the fields to a small river, where the kids played and threw stones into the water.

I felt really relaxed and happy that day. Living in the city, I rarely see open fields or breathe such fresh air, and it was a nice change from my usual routine of working at a computer. It was also lovely to spend time with my niece and nephew and see how much they enjoyed being outdoors. On the train home, they both fell asleep, and I remember thinking that I should make more effort to get out of the city regularly.

question:
Describe a time when you taught someone how to do something.

You should say:
• who you taught
• what you taught
• how you taught it

and explain how you felt about teaching this person.

You will have to talk about the topic for one to two minutes. You have one minute to think about what you are going to say. You can make some notes to help you if you wish.
answer:
I'd like to talk about the time I taught my grandfather how to use a smartphone. This was about a year and a half ago, after he received a phone as a present from my parents for his eightieth birthday.

At first, he was quite reluctant. He'd always used a very basic mobile phone that could only make calls, and he said he was too old to learn anything new. But my cousins live abroad, and I told him that if he learned to make video calls, he'd be able to see their children, his great-grandchildren, whenever he wanted. That convinced him.

I visited him every Sunday afternoon for about two months. I realised quickly that I needed to be very patient and go slowly. Things that seem obvious to me, like swiping or the meaning of different icons, were completely new to him. So I focused on just one or two things each week. First, I taught him how to unlock the phone and make a normal call. Then we moved on to sending messages, taking photos and finally making video calls. I also wrote simple step-by-step instructions on a piece of paper, with drawings, so that he could practise during the week.

At the beginning, I sometimes felt a bit frustrated, because he forgot things and needed me to repeat them many times. But overall, it was a very rewarding experience. I'll never forget his face the first time he made a video call to my cousin and saw the children waving at him. He was so happy. Now he sends me photos of his garden almost every day!
